questions.title: Hypoproteinemia in chronic liver disease's oedema
questions.question: A 55 years old man had chronic liver disease. On examination, there is bilateral pitting edema of the leg and ascites. Which of the following findings is most likely to be expected?

explanations.A: Correct. In chronic liver disease, impaired hepatic synthetic function reduces plasma albumin production, producing hypoproteinemia. The resulting fall in plasma oncotic pressure allows fluid to leak from the vasculature into the interstitium and peritoneal cavity, producing bilateral pitting leg oedema and ascites. Leukocytosis, hypertension and hypercalcaemia are not the expected accompanying findings of this hypoalbuminemic mechanism.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Leukocytosis reflects an inflammatory or infective process, not the hypoalbuminemic mechanism behind hepatic oedema and ascites.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Chronic liver disease more typically produces hypotension, from reduced oncotic pressure and vasodilation, than hypertension.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Hypercalcaemia is not a recognised feature of chronic liver disease's oedema and ascites; the expected biochemical finding is a low, not high, plasma protein level.

questions.title: Subdural fluid collection is a hematoma
questions.question: A 78-year-old woman falls in the bathtub and strikes the back of her head. Over the next 24 hours, she becomes increasingly somnolent. A head CT scan shows an accumulation of fluid beneath the dura, compressing the left cerebral hemisphere. Which of the following terms best describes this collection of fluid?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Congestion describes passive venous engorgement of blood within vessels, not a discrete extravasated collection outside them.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Petechiae are pinpoint haemorrhagic spots in skin or mucosa, not a large fluid collection compressing the brain.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Ecchymosis is a flat subcutaneous bruise, not a discrete, space-occupying fluid collection.
explanations.D: Correct. A localized collection of extravasated blood outside the vessel wall, such as the fluid accumulating beneath the dura after head trauma, compressing the underlying brain, is termed a hematoma. This is distinct from congestion, a passive venous engorgement within vessels, and from petechiae and ecchymosis, neither of which describes a discrete space-occupying collection. The elderly patient's delayed somnolence after a fall fits the classic evolving picture of such a hematoma.

questions.title: Ecchymosis is internal, not external, haemorrhage
questions.question: All are forms of external haemorrhage Except:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Haematuria, blood in the urine, is a form of external haemorrhage, since the blood exits the body through the urinary tract.
explanations.B: Correct. External haemorrhage describes blood loss that exits the body through a natural passage or surface, such as haematuria, haematemesis, epistaxis and haemoptysis. Ecchymosis, a larger flat subcutaneous bruise from blood extravasating into the skin and soft tissue, remains contained within the body. It is therefore a form of internal, not external, haemorrhage, unlike the other four options.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Haematemesis, vomited blood, is a form of external haemorrhage, exiting the body through the mouth.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Epistaxis, a nosebleed, is a form of external haemorrhage, exiting the body through the nose.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Haemoptysis, coughed-up blood, is a form of external haemorrhage, exiting the body through the airway and mouth.

questions.title: Lymphatic obstruction causes local oedema
questions.question: An example of local edema:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Cardiac disease raises systemic venous hydrostatic pressure throughout the body, producing generalized, not local, oedema.
explanations.B: Correct. Cardiac, renal and hepatic disease each raise venous or capsular hydrostatic pressure, or lower plasma oncotic pressure, systemically, producing generalized oedema. Lymphatic obstruction, by contrast, blocks fluid drainage from a specific, localized territory only, such as a single limb. This makes lymphatic obstruction the example of local, rather than generalized, oedema among these four causes.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Renal disease lowers plasma oncotic pressure, or raises circulating volume, systemically, producing generalized, not local, oedema.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Hepatic disease lowers plasma albumin systemically, producing generalized, not local, oedema.

questions.learning_objective: Identify lymphatic obstruction as an example of local oedema, contrasted with the generalized-oedema mechanisms of cardiac, renal and hepatic disease.

questions.title: Cardiac oedema starts in the legs
questions.question: cardiac edema starts in :

explanations.A: Incorrect. The chest is not the most gravity-dependent site in an ambulant patient, so it is not where cardiac oedema first appears.
explanations.B: Correct. Cardiac (congestive heart failure) oedema is a gravity-dependent oedema: raised systemic venous hydrostatic pressure from right-heart failure pushes fluid out of capillaries preferentially at the most dependent body site. In an ambulant patient, that site is the legs and ankles, not the chest, hand or face. This is why cardiac oedema is classically described as starting in the legs and worsening through the day.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The hand is not the most gravity-dependent site in an ambulant patient.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The face is a non-dependent site in an ambulant patient; facial oedema is more typical of a renal (nephritic), not cardiac, cause.

questions.title: Exudate clots on standing (high protein)
questions.question: Exudate is characterised by:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Poor protein content describes a transudate, not an exudate, which is protein-rich.
explanations.B: Correct. An inflammatory exudate has high protein content, including fibrinogen, which allows the fluid to clot on standing. A transudate, by contrast, has low protein content, a low specific gravity and few cells, and does not clot. Clotting on standing is therefore the characteristic that identifies an exudate among these four options.
explanations.C: Incorrect. A low specific gravity describes a transudate; an exudate's high protein content gives it a high specific gravity.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Scanty cells describe a transudate; an exudate is typically rich in inflammatory cells.

questions.learning_objective: State that an exudate clots on standing because of its high, fibrinogen-containing protein content, distinguishing it from a transudate's low-protein, non-clotting profile.

questions.title: Chronic small blood loss causes anemia
questions.question: Frequent loss of a small amount of blood may result in:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Thrombosis is the formation of a blood clot within a vessel, unrelated to the consequence of chronic external or internal blood loss.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Embolism is a detached mass travelling in the bloodstream to lodge elsewhere, not a consequence of chronic small-volume blood loss.
explanations.C: Correct. Repeated, small-volume blood loss over a long period does not reduce circulating blood volume acutely enough to trigger shock. Instead, the sustained loss of red cell mass and iron over time results in anemia, typically an iron-deficiency anemia. Thrombosis and embolism are unrelated consequences of ongoing external or internal blood loss.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Shock results from a large, acute reduction in circulating blood volume, not from repeated small losses over a long period.

questions.topic: Heamodynamic disorders: Gangrene, heamorhage and edema

questions.title: Cardiac ascitic fluid is a low-protein transudate
questions.question: In cardiac oedema:

options.A: the ascitic fluid clots on standing
options.B: the ascitic fluid has low protein content
options.C: the ascitic fluid show numerous cells
options.D: specific gravity of the extracellular fluid is more than 1015

explanations.A: Incorrect. Clotting on standing is a feature of a protein-rich exudate, not the low-protein transudate of cardiac oedema.
explanations.B: Correct. The ascitic fluid of cardiac oedema, from raised systemic and portal venous hydrostatic pressure in right-heart failure, is a transudate. It has low protein content, does not clot on standing, contains few cells, and has a specific gravity below 1015. This is the opposite fluid profile from an inflammatory exudate.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Numerous cells are a feature of an exudate, not the sparsely cellular transudate of cardiac oedema.
explanations.D: Incorrect. A specific gravity above 1015 is a feature of an exudate; cardiac oedema's transudate has a specific gravity below 1015.

questions.title: Malnutrition causes generalized oedema
questions.question: Oedema is generalized in:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Allergy produces a localized reaction at the site of exposure, not generalized oedema.
explanations.B: Correct. Malnutrition lowers plasma protein (albumin) synthesis systemically, reducing plasma oncotic pressure throughout the vasculature and producing generalized oedema. Allergy, acute inflammation and lymphatic obstruction, by contrast, each act at a localized site: a specific reaction, an inflamed area, or a blocked drainage territory. This produces local, rather than generalized, oedema for those three.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Acute inflammation produces localized oedema at the site of injury, not a generalized systemic oedema.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Chronic lymphatic obstruction blocks drainage from a specific territory, producing local, not generalized, oedema.

questions.title: Hydrogen sulphide causes gangrene's odour
questions.question: The tissue affected by gangrene has a bad odour because of:

explanations.A: Incorrect. The sheer number of organisms present is not itself what produces the odour; it is the specific putrefactive gas they generate.
explanations.B: Correct. Gangrenous tissue's characteristic bad odour is produced by hydrogen sulphide and other volatile compounds generated by putrefactive bacteria as they break down dead tissue. This is a specific chemical mechanism, not simply the raw quantity of organisms present, the degree of tissue destruction, or the level of systemic toxemia. Hydrogen sulphide production is therefore what accounts for the odour.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Tissue destruction describes the extent of damage, not the chemical source of the characteristic bad odour.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Toxemia describes the systemic absorption of bacterial toxins, not the local chemical source of the tissue's odour.

questions.title: Hemothorax is internal haemorrhage
questions.question: Which of the following is a type of internal haemorrhage:

explanations.A: Incorrect. A haematoma is a localized extravasated-blood collection, typically in skin or soft tissue, not specifically bleeding into a body cavity.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Purpura is a pattern of small subcutaneous or mucosal haemorrhages, not bleeding into a body cavity.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Ecchymosis is a flat subcutaneous bruise, not bleeding into a body cavity.
explanations.D: Correct. Internal haemorrhage describes bleeding contained within a body (serous) cavity, such as hemothorax, blood in the pleural cavity. Haematoma, purpura, ecchymosis and petechiae are skin or subcutaneous bleeding patterns of varying size, not bleeding into a body cavity. Hemothorax is therefore the example of internal haemorrhage among these five options.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Petechiae are pinpoint subcutaneous or mucosal haemorrhages, not bleeding into a body cavity.

questions.learning_objective: Identify hemothorax as internal haemorrhage, blood within a body cavity, distinguishing it from the skin/subcutaneous bleeding patterns haematoma, purpura, ecchymosis and petechiae.

questions.title: Lymphatic oedema is non-pitting
questions.question: Which of the following type of oedema is non-pitting:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Cardiac oedema, driven by raised hydrostatic pressure, remains pitting.
explanations.B: Correct. Lymphatic oedema is classically non-pitting: the protein-rich fluid that accumulates when lymphatic drainage is obstructed stimulates chronic fibrosis in the affected tissue, so pressure does not leave a persistent indentation. Cardiac, nutritional and nephritic oedema, driven by hydrostatic-pressure or oncotic-pressure mechanisms rather than protein-rich lymphatic stasis, remain pitting. This fibrotic, protein-rich mechanism is what makes lymphatic oedema the non-pitting exception.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Nutritional oedema, driven by low plasma oncotic pressure from hypoproteinemia, remains pitting.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Nephritic oedema, driven by fluid retention and altered oncotic and hydrostatic pressure, remains pitting.

questions.learning_objective: State that lymphatic oedema is non-pitting, from protein-rich fluid driving tissue fibrosis, unlike the pitting oedema of cardiac, nutritional and nephritic causes.

questions.title: Volvulus produces moist gangrene
questions.question: Which of the following types of gangrene occur as a result of torsion or twisting of intestines seen in a volvulus?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Senile gangrene is a form of dry gangrene from age-related atherosclerosis, an arterial-occlusion-alone mechanism, not the combined arterial-and-venous occlusion of a volvulus.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Gas gangrene results from Clostridium infection producing gas within tissue, a distinct infective mechanism, not the mechanical torsion of a volvulus.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Dry gangrene results from arterial occlusion alone, without the venous engorgement that a volvulus's combined torsion produces.
explanations.D: Correct. Torsion or twisting of the intestine, as in a volvulus, compresses and occludes both the venous and arterial supply to the affected loop. Because venous outflow is blocked as well as arterial inflow, the bowel becomes engorged with stagnant blood, favouring rapid bacterial putrefaction. This is the mechanism of moist, not dry, gas or senile, gangrene.
